part_title: AWS History, Global Infrastructure and Regional Design
review_basis: Visually inspected original AIF Module 02 WebPs slides 18–25, including AWS building blocks, global workloads, Region/AZ layout, decision criteria and edge caching.

scenes.title: How AWS cloud services developed
scenes.narration: This timeline provides historical context for why AWS offers infrastructure as reusable services. At the left, the slide starts with Amazon's internal efforts to standardize computing building blocks for its own operations. The next milestones describe the idea of offering those capabilities to other organizations. The middle and right highlight messaging, storage and compute services, followed by geographical expansion. Treat the years and launch descriptions as a high-level course illustration, not an authoritative current product chronology; current AWS product histories should be checked against official documentation if exact dates are required. The important technical ideas are below the timeline. Amazon EC2 provides virtual computing capacity: a company can request a server without buying a physical machine. Amazon S3 provides object storage, a way to save and retrieve files such as product images. Amazon SQS provides managed message queues. A queue is like a waiting line for work: a service places a message describing a task into the queue, and another program processes it later. Follow the online shop architecture at the bottom right. A customer opens the shopping application running on compute, the application retrieves product images from storage, and the order-handling process sends work into a queue. Background workers take order messages from that queue to update inventory or send confirmations. This separation is called decoupling, meaning one part does not need to finish all work synchronously before another part can respond. Consider a flash sale. Even when many orders arrive quickly, the queue can absorb tasks until workers have capacity, subject to configured limits. The takeaway is not to memorize every year. Understand that cloud platforms combine compute, storage and messaging into applications, and that you select each service for its job.

scenes.title: Understanding AWS global scale
scenes.narration: The large globe on this slide represents how AWS operates cloud infrastructure across many areas of the world. Lines connect locations, illustrating that an organization may serve users internationally instead of relying on a single building. On the right are four characteristics: worldwide infrastructure, a broad customer community, market presence and operational experience. These describe AWS's scale rather than guarantees that every service is available everywhere. Worldwide infrastructure helps a business place applications nearer its customers, but real performance also depends on network paths and application design. The everyday example at the bottom compares a cloud platform to a coffee chain that operates branches in different cities. Customers appreciate having a branch closer to them. Similarly, a website may respond faster when its application or cached content is nearer to the user. The analogy has limits: a cloud Region is not literally one store, and an online application may still have to retrieve data from another Region. Later slides distinguish Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations, which have different functions. If a company has customers in India and Europe, it may choose infrastructure to serve both groups appropriately. But a multi-Region design adds operating cost, synchronization and security responsibilities. The decision cue is to assess global reach alongside compliance, service support, resilience and actual cost. Here's a beginner question: if AWS has many global locations, does launching a database in one Region automatically copy it to every other Region? No. Data replication and regional deployments require deliberate configuration supported by the service.

scenes.title: Common workloads on the AWS Cloud
scenes.narration: A workload is simply a task or application that needs computing resources. This slide groups common workloads into four panels around the AWS cloud. The first is enterprise IT, meaning internal business applications such as human resources, finance and collaboration tools. The second is backup and storage, which protects information by retaining copies that can be used for recovery. Backup is not the same as high availability. A backup helps restore lost or damaged data, while high availability focuses on continuing service despite failure. The third panel is big data analytics. Analytics means examining data to discover patterns, trends or useful measurements. A retailer could study its sales history to identify the most popular products. The fourth panel includes websites, mobile applications and games. Their demand may rise suddenly, so cloud scaling can help when configured well. Now look at the example at the bottom. A growing business can host its website, back up its information, analyze user behavior and run employee applications using services from one provider. That doesn't mean it should put every component on the same machine or allow every employee to access all data. Each workload needs appropriate storage, identity permissions, monitoring and recovery plans. AI can appear across these categories. For example, an analytics team might forecast demand, a website might add a customer assistant, and a support team might classify incoming tickets. These are different applications that reuse cloud foundations. Quick check: if a company wants to restore its files after someone accidentally deletes them, is that primarily a backup-and-recovery requirement or a website-scaling requirement? Backup and recovery. Starting from the workload helps you choose the right services.

scenes.title: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations
scenes.narration: This architecture contains several geographical concepts, so follow its labeled flow. On the far left, a user requests a website or image. The request may reach an edge location, drawn next to the user. An edge location is a network location used by services such as content delivery to serve supported content closer to viewers. In the center-right is an AWS Region, which is a distinct geographical area where AWS offers regional services. Inside that Region are multiple Availability Zones, labeled AZ A, AZ B and AZ C. Each Availability Zone contains one or more separate data centers with independent infrastructure. The zoomed box on the far right shows a physical data center: the actual building housing servers, storage and network equipment. The difference matters. A Region is not one computer, an Availability Zone is not another name for a Region, and an edge location is not necessarily where your application database lives. Consider an online education site. Its application and student database might run in a selected Region, with copies or components across multiple Availability Zones to improve resilience. Frequently requested lesson images could be cached at edge locations closer to students. If the content is in the cache, it may return quickly. If not, the service fetches it from the configured origin. The origin is the source where the content is stored or generated. This picture illustrates an arrangement, not a requirement that every request passes through every box. Ask two questions. Where do we place the main application and regional database? In an appropriate AWS Region. Why use multiple Availability Zones? To reduce dependence on one failure location.

scenes.title: What is an AWS Region?
scenes.narration: Start with the globe showing labels such as us-east-1 and eu-west-3. These are example AWS Region identifiers, not IP addresses or separate customer accounts. A Region is a geographic area in which AWS operates infrastructure for supported services. Next, the middle image shows several data center buildings grouped within a Region. More precisely, a Region contains multiple Availability Zones, and each Availability Zone contains one or more data centers. The diagram simplifies those boundaries to explain the geography. On the right are two separate sets of resources, one in a US Region and another in a European Region. A storage resource created in one Region is not automatically the same storage resource as one created in another. Many AWS services are Region-scoped, while some services or control-plane features are global. Therefore always check a particular service's scope. Imagine creating an image-processing application in a US Region. If you also want the application running in a European Region, you may have to deploy supported components and arrange data movement or replication there. This is not the same as adding another Availability Zone within the original Region. The slide's bottom example emphasizes that separate regional deployments involve separate resources. A Region choice affects how far data travels, where information may be processed or stored, service availability and cost. The beginner check: if I upload a file into a regional storage service in one Region, should I assume AWS automatically makes a usable copy in every Region? No. Use the service's replication features when the design requires them.

scenes.title: Choosing the right AWS Region
scenes.narration: This slide gives us four practical questions to answer before selecting a Region. First, compliance and data requirements. Compliance means following relevant legal, contractual and organizational rules. Data residency refers to where information is stored or processed, and a selected Region alone may not resolve all residency requirements if services move or process data elsewhere. Check the actual service behavior. Second, proximity to customers. A Region closer to most users may lower network delay, which is called latency. For a real-time application, a shorter delay can make it feel more responsive. Third, service availability. Not every AWS service, model or feature is offered in every Region, so check that the resources your design needs are supported. Fourth, pricing. Costs can differ between Regions, and data transfer between locations can introduce additional charges. The example at the bottom uses an online store. First confirm applicable privacy requirements, then consider where customers are located, whether the required services exist, and which candidate Region has a suitable total cost. Think of choosing a university campus location: you consider rules, travel distance, available facilities and expense together. You should not choose only the cheapest campus if it lacks the required program. Similarly, the lowest-priced cloud Region is not automatically the best solution. A good decision documents why it was selected and revisits the assumption when workloads change. Quick check: a service is unavailable in your nearest Region. Is proximity alone sufficient reason to deploy there? No. A missing required service may force an alternative architecture or Region.

scenes.title: What is an Availability Zone?
scenes.narration: The slide's right-hand diagram shows one AWS Region divided into three Availability Zones, labeled ap-southeast-2a, 2b and 2c for illustration. Each box represents a separate infrastructure location within the same Region. The buildings are connected by a high-bandwidth, low-latency network, which means they can communicate quickly while remaining physically separated. The three numbered explanations on the left are important. First, an Availability Zone belongs to a Region. Second, zones are designed to isolate many infrastructure failures, because they use separate physical facilities and power and networking arrangements. Third, zones are connected well enough for applications to distribute components across them. Why would we pay attention to this? Imagine a college examination portal used by thousands of students. If every application server runs in one zone and that zone experiences a problem, the portal may become unavailable. Placing correctly configured application capacity in more than one zone can reduce that risk. But merely putting two servers in two zones does not ensure high availability; the application, routing, database and recovery strategy also need to work when a zone fails. The bottom analogy compares separated buildings in a city with reliable connections between them. Another important detail: a zone label like the letter a can map to different physical zones across AWS accounts in some configurations, so use appropriate zone identifiers when exact cross-account alignment matters. For AI inference endpoints or supporting services, choose a supported multi-AZ design where available. The exam-style answer: if you need protection against an entire Availability Zone failing within a Region, design across multiple zones, not just more servers in the same zone.

scenes.title: Edge locations and content delivery
scenes.narration: Follow the long picture from the person on the left toward the AWS origin on the right. The end user requests a file, such as an image on a website or part of an instructional video. The first stop in this illustrative content-delivery design is a nearby edge location. An edge location can keep a cached copy of reusable content. A cache is temporary storage of information so the system can return it faster next time. If the requested file is already at that edge, the service can respond without going all the way back to the source. If the content is not there, it may be obtained through a regional cache or from the origin in an AWS Region. The regional cache, shown in the middle-right, can serve a wider group of edge locations. The origin on the far right is the actual source configured for the application. AWS CloudFront is a content delivery service that uses edge infrastructure. The picture simplifies the actual cache hierarchy; not every request uses every tier. Why is this useful? Imagine students around the world opening the same course diagram. Serving copies closer to them can reduce waiting time and decrease repeat requests to the origin. But not all content should be shared in a cache. Personalized exam results, private account records and individual AI responses need careful authentication and cache-key rules to avoid giving one user another's information. The slide's decision cue says use edge locations when lower content-delivery latency matters, especially for a global audience. A quick check: does an edge location replace the main regional database? No. It usually helps deliver eligible content close to users, while the source application and data follow their own architecture.
